title: Composing tasks
summary: Run several operations at the same time, wait for all of them or the first of them, and handle their failures.

steps.title: Starting is not awaiting
body: Calling an async method **starts** the work and hands you a task straight away. `await` is a separate step: it waits for a task that is already running.
Usually you do both on one line, so the operations run one after another:
```csharp
int tea = await GetStockAsync("TEA");   // start, wait 50 ms
int mug = await GetStockAsync("MUG");   // then start, wait 50 ms   -> about 100 ms
That is **sequential**. If the second call does not need the result of the first, you are waiting for nothing. Start both first, then await:
```csharp
Task<int> teaTask = GetStockAsync("TEA");   // started
Task<int> mugTask = GetStockAsync("MUG");   // started too; both are now in progress
int tea = await teaTask;
int mug = await mugTask;                    // -> about 50 ms in total
That is **concurrent**: the two waits overlap. The waiter handed in two orders and the kitchen is working on both.

steps.prompt: An async method runs like a normal method until its first `await`. What does this print?
code: static async Task<string> FetchAsync(string name, int ms)
steps.explain: Each call prints its `start` line and returns a task as soon as it reaches the delay. `B` finishes first, but the program awaits `a` first, so `A` is printed first. Awaiting `b` afterwards returns at once: it was already done.

steps.prompt: `LoadAsync` takes about 50 ms. Roughly how long does each version take?
options: Version 1 about 150 ms, version 2 about 50 ms
Version 1 about 50 ms, version 2 about 150 ms
steps.explain: Version 1 only starts each load after the previous one has finished: 50 + 50 + 50. Version 2 starts all three before waiting, so the three waits overlap.

steps.title: Task.WhenAll
body: `Task.WhenAll` takes several tasks and gives you **one** task that finishes when all of them have finished.
```csharp
Task<int> teaTask = GetStockAsync("TEA");
Task<int> mugTask = GetStockAsync("MUG");
int[] stock = await Task.WhenAll(teaTask, mugTask);
// stock[0] is the TEA result, stock[1] is the MUG result
When the tasks are all `Task<T>`, awaiting `WhenAll` gives a `T[]`. The results are in the order you **passed the tasks**, not the order they finished.
It also accepts any sequence of tasks, so it pairs well with `Select`:
```csharp
List<string> skus = ...;
int[] stock = await Task.WhenAll(skus.Select(sku => GetStockAsync(sku)));
`Select` calls `GetStockAsync` for every sku, which starts them all. `WhenAll` waits for the lot.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so both lookups run at the same time and `total` is the combined stock.
steps.explain: `Task.WhenAll` combines the two tasks. Awaiting it gives an `int[]` with both results, and `Sum()` adds them.

steps.title: Stop queueing
prompt: The harness provides `Warehouse.GetStockAsync(string sku)`, which returns a `Task<int>` and takes about 30 ms per call.
`TotalStockAsync` gives the right answer, but it asks for one sku at a time. With 3 skus that is 90 ms; with 300 it is 9 seconds.
Change it so **all the lookups are in progress at the same time**. The harness counts how many calls overlap.
template: Dojo.Eq("TotalStockAsync(TEA, MUG, POT) is 47", 47, await TotalStockAsync(new List<string> { "TEA", "MUG", "POT" }));
Dojo.Eq("all 3 lookups were in progress at the same time", 3, Warehouse.MaxInFlight);
Dojo.Eq("each sku was looked up once", 3, Warehouse.Calls);
Dojo.Eq("TotalStockAsync of no skus is 0", 0, await TotalStockAsync(new List<string>()));
public static async Task<int> GetStockAsync(string sku)
hints: The `await` inside the loop is the problem: each lookup only starts after the one before it has finished.
Start them all first: `skus.Select(sku => Warehouse.GetStockAsync(sku))` gives a sequence of tasks.

steps.title: Task.WhenAny
body: `Task.WhenAny` finishes as soon as the **first** of its tasks finishes. Use it to race things: two mirror servers, or real work against a timer.
```csharp
Task<string> eu = DownloadAsync("eu-server");
Task<string> us = DownloadAsync("us-server");
Task<string> winner = await Task.WhenAny(eu, us);   // the task that finished first
string data = await winner;                          // its result
Awaiting `WhenAny` gives you the winning **task**, not its value. You await that task once more to get the result (or the exception, if the winner failed).
The other tasks are **not stopped**. They keep running; you are just no longer waiting for them.

code: static async Task<string> FromAsync(string server, int ms)
steps.explain: `us` only needs 5 ms, so it wins the race. At that moment `slow` is still running: `WhenAny` does not wait for the losers and does not cancel them.

steps.prompt: `A`, `B` and `LoadAsync` are async methods. Does each snippet run them one after another, or at the same time?
items: `var a = A(); var b = B(); await a; await b;`
steps.explain: Look for where the methods are *called*. If the second call only happens after an `await` on the first, it is sequential. If both are called before anything is awaited, they overlap.

steps.title: When a task fails
body: If an async method throws, the exception is stored **in its task**. It is thrown again at the point where you `await` that task, so an ordinary `try`/`catch` works:
```csharp
try
string page = await DownloadAsync(url);
catch (InvalidOperationException ex)
Console.WriteLine($"failed: {ex.Message}");

With `Task.WhenAll`, several tasks can fail. `WhenAll` still waits for **all** of them to finish. Then `await` throws the **first** exception only. The complete set is kept on the combined task, in `task.Exception`, which is an **`AggregateException`**: one exception that wraps many (`InnerExceptions`).
You will also meet `AggregateException` if you block on a task with `.Wait()` or `.Result`: those wrap even a single failure. `await` never does. That is one more reason to prefer `await`.
> **Tip:** If one failure should not sink the whole batch, catch it *inside* each task: wrap the call in a small async method with its own `try`/`catch` that returns a fallback.

steps.prompt: Both tasks fail. What does this print?
steps.explain: `await` rethrows just one of the original exceptions, with its real type. The combined task still remembers both, inside its `AggregateException`.

steps.title: Fetch them all
prompt: The harness provides `Web.GetAsync(string url)`, which returns a `Task<string>` with the page text. For a site that is down it throws an `InvalidOperationException`.
Returns the page text, or `failed: ` followed by the url if `Web.GetAsync` throws.
Fetches every url with `SafeGetAsync`, **all at the same time**, and returns the results in the same order as `urls`.
starter: // try the download; turn a failure into "failed: <url>"
// start every SafeGetAsync, then wait for all of them
template: Dojo.Eq("SafeGetAsync(\"shop\") returns the page", "page of shop", await SafeGetAsync("shop"));
Dojo.Eq("SafeGetAsync(\"bad-host\") returns failed: bad-host", "failed: bad-host", await SafeGetAsync("bad-host"));
Dojo.Eq("FetchAllAsync returns results in the order of the urls", new List<string> { "page of shop", "failed: bad-host", "page of blog", "page of docs" }, pages);
Dojo.Eq("all 4 downloads were in progress at the same time", 4, Web.MaxInFlight);
Dojo.Eq("each url was fetched once", 4, Web.Calls);
Dojo.Eq("FetchAllAsync of no urls is an empty list", 0, (await FetchAllAsync(new List<string>())).Count);
public static void Reset() { lock (Gate) { _inFlight = 0; MaxInFlight = 0; Calls = 0; } }
public static async Task<string> GetAsync(string url)
if (url.StartsWith("bad")) throw new InvalidOperationException(url + " is down");
hints: `SafeGetAsync`: put `return await Web.GetAsync(url);` inside a `try` block. The `await` has to be inside the `try`, because that is where the exception comes out.
`FetchAllAsync`: `string[] pages = await Task.WhenAll(urls.Select(url => SafeGetAsync(url)));` then `return pages.ToList();`. `WhenAll` keeps the order for you.
